summary:
New Zealand nationality and passport rules apply to the Cook Islands, while local criminal law governs conduct on the islands.

Sections 154 and 155 of the Cook Islands Crimes Act 1969 criminalised sexual activity between men and any indecent act with or upon another male, carrying maximum terms of seven years and five years respectively, with consent explicitly not a defence. Later coverage of the repeal cited a maximum of ten years for indecent acts between males. The penalty figures reported for the 1969 provisions differ across the sources, but all agree the offences were never enforced in living memory.

Parliament voted on Friday 14 April 2023 to strike the provisions from the Crimes Act through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023. A note attached to the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBT people in the Cook Islands, and the same bill added protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault. The repeal removed a colonial-era provision still on the statute books rather than an active prosecution threat.

Decriminalisation was stalled for years before 2023. A draft Crimes Bill, written with assistance from New Zealand, would have deleted sections 154 and 155, and a 2017 select committee recommended their removal; MPs subsequently backtracked on that recommendation. In 2020 parliament again deferred the bill's report by three months.

Same-sex marriage remains prohibited in the Cook Islands under the Marriage Amendment Act 2000. The islands' only LGBTI community organisation, the Te Tiare Association, campaigned for repeal across the whole period, and its members described the 1969 provisions as homophobia brought by colonisation into a society whose pre-contact history accepted same-sex relationships. The Cook Islands population was about 21,000 when the bill was drafted in 2017.
tangentialFactors:
The 2023 Crimes Amendment Bill did not repeal the same-sex offences in isolation. It carried a note on growing acceptance of LGBT people and simultaneously added legal protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault, so the repeal travelled with measures on unrelated offences in the same legislative package.

The repeal was drafted with help from New Zealand. The 2017 draft Crimes Bill was written with New Zealand assistance, which is consistent with the free-association arrangement under which Cook Islands criminal legislation is developed alongside New Zealand legal support.

Public submissions on the 2017 Crimes Bill opened in the Cook Islands Parliament. The clerk of Parliament, John Tangi, confirmed that a submission from the Te Tiare Association, representing the LGBTI community, was already before the select committee, and at least three lawyers were expected to address the committee on penalties and sentencing.

Colonial-era sexual offences carried long periods of dormancy in Cook Islands law: the provisions were retained in the statute book despite a decade of stalled bills and an evidentiary record of no enforcement, so the risk they represented was reputational and deterrent rather than practical.
localsOnly:
Te Tiare Association was the only LGBTI community group in the Cook Islands and led the decriminalisation campaign from the 2017 draft bill through the 2023 vote. Its members publicly described the 1969 offences as homophobia imported by colonisation into a historically accepting society.

The repeal campaign was pursued through Cook Islands parliamentary procedure: a 2017 select committee took submissions and recommended removal of sections 154 and 155, only for the bill to be deferred repeatedly, including a three-month deferral in 2020, before the April 2023 vote.

Residents travel and hold documents under New Zealand nationality and passport arrangements, while offences and offences law administered locally are those of the Cook Islands.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory addresses same-sex conduct only. It contains no information on the legal status of gender identity in the Cook Islands: no detail on legal gender recognition, on the marker requirements for Cook Islands residents travelling on New Zealand passports, or on how New Zealand identity-document procedures apply from the Cook Islands.

Nothing in the sources covers anti-discrimination protection, hate-crime provisions, restrictions or protections around bathrooms and other gendered facilities, or access to gender-affirming medical care for trans people in the Cook Islands.

The extension of New Zealand human-rights and human-rights-instrument protections to the Cook Islands is not addressed in the inventory; how much of New Zealand's framework applies to residents of a state in free association remains unresolved on this record.

Enforcement, sentencing and complaint-handling data after the 1 June 2023 repeal are not available here, as are entry and visa rules applying to trans visitors, or any reporting on anti-trans violence with dates or outcomes.
